Title: The Weight of White Space
Abstract: Empty space is not empty at all. In this thesis I trace the history of margin, silence, and pause in printed matter—from medieval manuscripts to modernist grid systems—and ask what happens when we stop filling.

Title: Vernacular Futures
Abstract: Folk aesthetics have always leaked into design whether we invite them or not. I follow the trail of vernacular letterforms across Dutch street signage, market stalls, and amateur-printed flyers to find a design language that was never taught in any school.

Title: Dust and Data
Abstract: I grew up in a house full of printed receipts, torn calendars, and handwritten notes stuck to the fridge with magnets shaped like fruit. This thesis is about the graphic archaeology of the everyday home.

Title: Translation as Design
Abstract: Every act of translation is also an act of design. I look at Japanese-English bilingual publishing from the 1960s to now, asking how the space between two scripts becomes a site of negotiation, compromise, and sometimes invention.

Title: Infrastructures of Attention
Abstract: Before anyone reads a poster, the poster has already spoken. I map the invisible design decisions that determine what we notice, what we ignore, and who gets to make that choice in public space.

Title: Color Has No Memory
Abstract: A study of how color meaning migrates across cultures and decades. Starting from a single shade of green found in both a Guinean ceremonial cloth and a Dutch pharmaceutical label, I unravel the surprisingly short distances between very different worlds.

Title: The Error as Method
Abstract: Glitch, misprint, and accident have been systematically excluded from the design canon. This thesis rehabilitates the mistake as a productive force, drawing on case studies from offset printing disasters that became collector's items.

Title: Cookbook as Archive
Abstract: The cookbook is the most widely read genre of nonfiction and the least studied. I treat recipes as designed objects—layouts of time, quantity, and gesture—and ask what they preserve that photographs cannot.

Title: Surface Tension
Abstract: I spent three months photographing the underside of tables in public libraries. This thesis uses those images as a starting point for thinking about surfaces that face away, graphic matter that was never meant to be seen.

Title: Grief in Lowercase
Abstract: Death notices, condolence cards, memorial pages—typographic conventions for grief are remarkably stable across time. I ask why mourning looks the way it does, and what it would mean to design it differently.

Title: The Second Grid
Abstract: The baseline grid is a promise the designer makes to the reader. But what about the invisible secondary structures—optical margins, hang zones, bleed relationships—that no software makes visible? This thesis names and maps them.

Title: Patterns Without Origin
Abstract: Geometric pattern is often described as Islamic, Celtic, or Scandinavian—but pattern travels faster than attribution. Tracing a single motif across four continents and six centuries, I follow what happens to form when it leaves its supposed source.

Title: Instructions for Disappearing
Abstract: The exit sign is the most-designed and least-noticed object in any building. I use it as a lens to examine emergency graphics—a typographic genre governed entirely by fear, liability, and international standards.

Title: Softness as Argument
Abstract: Rounded corners, pastel gradients, cushioned typefaces—the visual language of care and wellness has become the visual language of everything. I trace how softness became a political aesthetic and ask what it costs.

Title: Mediterranean Miscellany
Abstract: A collection of menus, wine labels, bus tickets, and film posters gathered from a single square kilometer in Naples over the course of a summer. This thesis argues that graphic density is a form of urban memory.

Title: Paper Remembers
Abstract: Different papers age differently. I investigate the material life of printed documents—how acid content, humidity, and light transform graphic artifacts over decades—and ask whether designers have a responsibility to time.

Title: The Margin Note
Abstract: Readers have always written back. This thesis studies marginalia across centuries—annotations, corrections, arguments, drawings—as a counter-design practice that reveals what official layouts suppress.

Title: Alphabet Soup
Abstract: I was five years old when I first understood that Greek and Latin letters were cousins who had stopped speaking. This thesis is a personal and typographic history of the moment children encounter a second alphabet.

Title: Propaganda Geometry
Abstract: The triangle points. The fist rises. The sun radiates. Political graphics share a remarkably small vocabulary of shapes. I catalog and analyze the geometric grammar of persuasion across movements that otherwise had nothing in common.

Title: The Folded Page
Abstract: Before the accordion book, the leporello, and the zine, there was just a piece of paper someone folded. I trace the phenomenology of the fold as a design act—the way it creates sequence, reveals and conceals, and turns surface into space.

Title: Sans-Serif Century
Abstract: The twentieth century chose the sans-serif and never looked back. Or did it? This thesis examines the persistent return of serif typography in modernist graphic design—the footnote that keeps refusing to disappear.

Title: Catalogue of Distances
Abstract: I collected every distance printed on a road sign within a ten kilometer radius of my childhood home in Taichung. The resulting dataset became a meditation on measurement, place, and the arbitrary precision of wayfinding.

Title: The Poster Sleeps
Abstract: What happens to a poster at three in the morning when nobody is looking? I spent forty nights photographing the same wall in Moscow at regular intervals, building an archive of presence and absence as a study in graphic temporality.

Title: Against Clarity
Abstract: Clarity is not a neutral value. This thesis questions the modernist ideal of transparent communication, arguing that obscurity, ambiguity, and difficulty have been essential to graphic practice—and that their elimination is a political act.

Title: The Stamp Speaks
Abstract: Postage stamps are the smallest official graphic objects a state produces. I read them as condensed ideologies—compressed landscapes, portraits, and symbols that tell the story of what a government wants to be remembered for.

Title: Handwriting in Crisis
Abstract: Cursive is disappearing from school curricula across Europe. I document the last generation of children taught to write by hand in three countries, asking what is lost when the body's relationship to the letter is severed.

Title: Neon and Shadow
Abstract: The neon sign is a dying medium. I spent a year photographing working neon installations across Spain before their owners replaced them with LED panels, building an archive of a light technology that made cities illegible in the best possible way.

Title: Topography of Care
Abstract: Hospital wayfinding systems are designed for panic. I redesign them for calm—rethinking color-coding, icon families, and floor numbering systems based on interviews with patients, visitors, and cleaning staff who actually navigate them.

Title: The Script That Refused
Abstract: Arabic script was declared incompatible with the printing press, the typewriter, and the personal computer—and survived all three. This thesis follows the engineers, calligraphers, and activists who refused each incompatibility verdict.

Title: Colour of Money
Abstract: Currency design is the most constrained and most consequential graphic design there is. I analyze the visual evolution of the Euro banknote series across three decades, reading its bridges and windows as documents of political imagination.

Title: The Sheet Before Printing
Abstract: Paper is already designed before anything is printed on it. This thesis investigates the prehistory of the printed page—watermarks, chain lines, laid patterns—as graphic information that precedes and outlasts the press.
